opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, before I actually had to make the decision, I think I cared about rankings a lot more than I'd like to admit. When you're young, and especially coming from the kind of education system I grew up in, rankings feel like the only objective signal you have. You look at a list, you see a number, and it gives you a kind of comfort. You think, okay, if I get into a place that's higher on this list, then my future is more or less secured.

But the more I thought about it, and the more I talked to people who were a few years ahead of me, the more I realized the ranking of a school is a very coarse measure. What actually matters, especially for research, is much more local: who your advisor is, what the lab culture is like, whether the people around you are excited about the same problems, and whether you'll have the freedom to explore. A top-ranked school with an advisor who isn't a good fit can be a much worse experience than a slightly lower-ranked school where you find the right mentor and the right group of peers.

So my thinking gradually shifted from "Which school is the best?" to "Where will I grow the most?" Those are really different questions. I also think there's some anxiety in worrying about rankings, this fear that one decision will define the rest of your life. In hindsight, that's rarely true. What defines your trajectory is what you actually do once you're there: the work you choose, the risks you're willing to take, the people you learn from.

That said, I don't want to pretend rankings mean nothing. They correlate with resources, with the density of talented people, with opportunities. It's reasonable to take them into account. I just think they should be one input among many, not the deciding factor. If I could talk to my younger self, I'd say: don't let the number make the choice for you. Go find the people you want to work with.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he cared about rankings a lot before making the decision, which contradicts the criterion that he saw little reason to worry about them.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I was applying for my PhD, I didn't think about rankings as much as people might assume. I came from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and like a lot of students at that stage, I knew the big names, but what I actually cared about was who I would be working with. In our field, your advisor and your lab matter far more than the overall rank of the school. A top-ranked university where you don't have a good fit with an advisor can be a much worse outcome than a slightly lower-ranked place where someone is genuinely invested in you and the research direction is exciting.

Of course, I would be lying if I said rankings didn't enter my mind at all. There's a certain social pressure, especially coming from a Chinese background, where people around you, your family, your classmates, talk about these lists. But I think I was fairly clear-headed that rankings are a very coarse signal. They average over many departments and many things that have nothing to do with your day-to-day life as a researcher.

So what I did was look at the people. Who was publishing work I found interesting, who had students that seemed to be doing well, what the culture of the group felt like. I ended up at UC San Diego, which is a wonderful place but perhaps not the first name people think of, and working with Zhuowen Tu was one of the best decisions I made. It shaped how I think about research even today.

In hindsight, I'd tell students the same thing: rankings are something you worry about before you choose, and then once you're in, they almost completely disappear. What stays is the research, the people, and whether you're growing.

r001.rationale: He says rankings mattered less to him than people might assume and that advisor and lab fit mattered far more, conveying little concern about rankings while choosing.

astra-6.text: Before I actually had to choose, rankings felt like a big deal. They gave me a simple way to compare schools when I didn’t really know how else to evaluate them. I worried that going to a lower-ranked school might mean fewer opportunities later. But I didn’t have a very concrete understanding of that—I was mostly treating the ranking as a proxy for how good the experience would be.

r001.rationale: The response says rankings felt like a big deal and that he worried about the consequences of choosing a lower-ranked school, rather than conveying little reason to worry.

sol-6.1.text: Before I actually had to make that choice, rankings felt pretty important. They were a straightforward way to compare schools when I didn’t know much else about them. But I think there’s a difference between a school’s overall reputation and whether it’s the right place for you to do research. As the decision gets more concrete, you start asking different questions: Who would I work with? What problems could I work on? Would I learn a lot in that environment? So I wouldn’t say rankings meant nothing to me, but they weren’t enough to make the decision.

r001.rationale: The candidate says rankings felt “pretty important” before the choice, contradicting the criterion that he saw little reason to worry about them.
